349.prule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the stem, whatever precedes it in the word: prefixes and proclitics are unstressed (ˈpǎhnį 'shirt', rą̀ˈpǎhnį 'the shirt', ną̀rą̀ˈpǎhnį 'this the shirt', díˈpède 'I am counting').
349.srule: Secondary stress is stated only for the few four-syllable stems: primary on the first stem syllable, secondary on the third stem syllable. No secondary stress or alternating rhythm is described for other stem lengths or for prefix/proclitic syllables; positions count from the stem, not the word edge.
349.quote: 8. The syllable with primary stress is the nucleus of the phonological word. There are a few four-syllable stems. With these words, primary stress occurs on the first syllable and a secondary stress (unmarked) on the third: ... A stressed syllable is perceived as slightly louder and slightly longer than other syllables

V. Pike…
349.exq_: It is the first syllable of a stem: ˈpǎhnį shirt, rą̀ˈpǎhnį the shirt, ną̀rą̀ˈpǎhnį this the shirt ... the article or possessive pronoun of a noun phrase when it follows another noun, or a verb, usually (except in slow speech) clusters with the preceding phonological word
349.tone: Three contrastive lexical tonemes (high, low, upglide) on all syllables except the prepause syllable (domain of intonation) and the final syllable of a multisyllabic stem; the upglide occurs only on stressed syllables. Tone coexists with stem-initial word stress, which the authors mark by length/loudness and describe separately.

tn.quote: 5. Lexical tone contrasts on all syllables except the prepause syllable, and the final syllable of a multisyllable stem. (Intonation is contrastive on the prepause syllable, see 6, and unless modified by intonation, a stem-final syllable has high tone.) There are three tonemes: high /´/, low /`/, and upglide /ˇ/. These contrastive tones cause a difference in meaning of lexical items, as in: díˈtų́hų I sing, díˈtų̀hų I plant … On the nonstressed syllables, only the contrast of high versus low tone occurs. That is, the upglide occurs only on stressed syllables

tn.note: Three lexical tonemes, high, low and upglide, contrast on every syllable except the prepause and stem-final syllables; upglide only on stressed syllables; separate stem-initial word stress.

morph.elicq: The stress section (3.4, p.36-37) gives no statement of how stress was determined. General methodology, sec. 1.5.3 p.10: 'I collected data primarily in four ways: elicitation, tape-recording stories and conversations, observing and participating in conversations, and written materials. The only evidence-type hint in the phonology is p.35: 'it is supported by the fact that a few Ternatean speakers inserted a glottal stop between word-final identical vowels when they were speaking slowly for me' (i.e. words elicited in isolation/slow speech). morph.stmt: Exclusively prefixing/procliticising with little morphology overall: 'In Ternatean, all affixes are prefixes, and each affix has a fixed position in word-formation' (Hayami-Allen 2001:12); 'Subject markers are all proclitics, and all affixes are prefixes' (p.15); 'Ternatean derivational morphology makes use of three processes: lenition, reduplication and prefixation. I have not found any suffixes in this language' (p.112); only 'the subject clitics and the possessive prefixes... seem to be inflectional' (p.112); verb template (5.1) p.113: (CAUS-)(ASP-/REFL-/RECIP-)(CAUS-)(REDP-)(LEN-)ROOT; the only post-head grammatical material is free stressed particles…

351.srule: Secondary stress falls on the initial syllable of the word if the word consists of two metrical feet: in words of four syllables, and in trisyllabic compounds and full reduplications whose underlying unstressed second syllable has been elided; reduplications and compounds carry two stresses, other words have secondary stress only if they consist of four syllables (van Klinken 1999 sec. 2.3.3 p. 18-19, sec. 2.3.4.2 p. 20).
351.quote: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Secondary stress falls on the initial syllable of the word, if the word consists of two metrical feet. This occurs in words of four syllables, as well as in trisyllabic compounds and full reduplications where the underlying unstressed second syllable has been elided (§2.10.5.2). Prefixes, partial reduplicants and clitics do not attract stress, and are not counted in stress assignment rules. (That is, they are extrametrical.) morph.rootq: §2.3.3 pp.18-19: 'Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Secondary stress falls on the initial syllable of the word, if the word consists of two metrical feet. ... Prefixes, partial reduplicants and clitics do not attract stress, and are not counted in stress assignment rules. (That is, they are extrametrical.) However, there are no syllabic suffixes and the only syllabic enclitic is possessive -kan, with the result that the only phonological words for which stress is antepenultimate are the possessive-marked pronouns.' (Table 2.5 lists '3: prefixed root ha-bádak make-short' and '3: with enclitic -kan há'u-kan'.)
morph.elicq: No statement of how lexical stress was determined. The grammar as a whole rests on a recorded text corpus: 'Some were willing to record, and these recordings form the basis of the observations in this grammar. Recordings totalled approximately 23 hours. Those texts which were fully transcribed ... totalled over 64,000 words' (§1.3.2 p.11); on stress itself only impressionistic remarks: 'Word stress seems to be realised mainly by loudness and pitch. The difference in strength between stressed and unstressed syllables varies considerably from one speaker and context to another.' (§2.3.3 p.19), with supporting evidence drawn from word games and poetry…
morph.stmt: Predominantly (lightly) prefixing: 'There are four reasonably productive derivational prefixes or prefix-suffix combinations, and no productive suffixes.... The only other inflection is subject marking on verbs, which takes the form of an initial consonantal prefix' (§1.4 p.12); 'Enclitics and suffixes consist of a single consonant (e.g. enclitic genitive -n, suffix nominaliser -n), with the exception of a single CVC enclitic (possessive -kan)' (§2.3.2.6 p.18); 'Tetun has little morphological marking of constructions' (§1.4 p.12), most grammatical categories (TAM, plural, definiteness, negation ha'i, interrogation) being free pre- or post-head words.

352.prule: No word-level count rule exists. True rule (Speirs 1966:75-77): heaviest stress falls on the ROOT-initial syllable, whatever the word's syllable count — nouns (root at the left word edge) stress syllable 1 ("témá, "agóyó, "púwéré); two-syllable verbs (monosyllabic prefix + monosyllabic base) stress syllable 2 (na"má/na"ná); three-syllable verbs stress syllable 2 (na"pówá, dó"yámú = 010, falsifying 100 as well as 10). tn.note: Three tonemes: high, low, glide (drawn as a fall); glide only on CV:, CVN, CV° syllables, never short CV. Speirs reanalyses Hoijer & Dozier's mid and weak; Yegerlehner gives Arizona Tewa two tones.

352.cfw: Speirs 1966, the only grammar of Tewa, reports decidedly heavier stress on the first syllable of level-toned CVCV nouns regardless of their position in the utterance and expressly rejects the equal-stress claim of Hoijer and Dozier 1949, a six-page preliminary sketch of the Santa Clara dialect based on a single bilingual speaker, while Sutton 2014 independently places Kiowa-Tanoan lexical stress on the first syllable of the stem.

353.dq: If the phrase has no sustained stress, the last syllable in the phrase has at least normal stress.
353.dloc: Noss 1964:31 §1.8.3 Phrase Morphophonemics (archive.org); §1.6 phonemic phrase defined by sustained stress
353.prule: Final, stated for the phonemic phrase: 'If the phrase has no sustained stress, the last syllable in the phrase has at least normal stress' (rule 1); 'All syllables with short duration have weak stress', e.g. /kra'paw/ 'pocket' (rule 4); other syllables have either weak or normal stress 'within the limitations of predictability' of sec. 1.8.2, where the morphemes that characteristically have weak stress (pronouns, classifiers, other minor form-class members) are listed (rule 5) (Noss 1964:31-32, sec. 1.8.3).
353.srule: Not mentioned in Noss 1964 (sec. 1.6.2, 1.8.3: phrase-level loud/normal/weak stress only). Later word-level studies state a secondary stress: primary on the final syllable, secondary on non-final heavy syllables (not on CVʔ / 'linker' Ca syllables), assigned by right-headed feet built leftward from the final stress (default 3-syl [ˌσ σ ˈσ], 4-syl [σ ˌσ σ ˈσ]) and optionally suppressed in casual or fast speech; in compounds, secondary stress on the head syllable of each non-final member.
353.quote: The rules for prediction of stress-onset in morphophonemically written phrases are re-stated as follows: 1) If the phrase has no sustained stress, the last syllable in the phrase has at least normal stress. Phonemic: /'klàb 'bâan ./ 'Went home.' Morphophonemic: /klab bâan ./ 2) If the phrase contains a sustained stress, the same syllable that has the sustained stress also has at least normal stress and the syllables after it have no more than weak stress. [...] 4) All syllables with short duration have weak stress. Phonemic: /kra 'paw/ 'pocket' Morphophonemic: /krapaw/
353.loc: p.31 §1.8.3 Phrase Morphophonemics, rule 1; p.32 rule 4
353.idn: standard spoken Thai (ST), the official language of Thailand / prestige dialect; informants included Central Plains (CP) dialect speakers as well as standard (ST) speakers; data: Field research in Thailand 1950-52 (Yale dissertation 'An Outline of Siamese Grammar', 1954) and summer 1961 (FSI); informants interviewed…
353.exq_: Most classes of lexemes consist of members which include normal stress in at least one syllable of some allolex (see 2.1.3.2.), but a few classes characteristically lack stress in all their forms - e.g. pronouns, prepositions, and certain kinds of classifiers.
353.tone: Six contrasting tones, 'four of them relatively level in contour, one falling, and one rising. There is no zero tone' (Noss 1964:7 sec. 1.2.5). Tone interacts with stress: under weak stress and medium-short or less duration, morphs with mid and low tone are replaced by toneless morphs, and morphs with constricted high, falling and rising tone are replaced by morphs with plain high tone (p.29 sec. 1.8.2 rules 4-5).

morph.rootq: Noss treats stress as phonemic per syllable and predicts stress-onset by position in the phonemic phrase and by rhythm (syllable duration), never by root/stem: §1.8.3 p.31 '1) If the phrase has no sustained stress, the last syllable in the phrase has at least normal stress. Phonemic: /'klàb 'bâan ./ 'Went home.' Morphophonemic: /klàb bâan ./'; '3) Syllables with medium-short duration which occur after syllables of the same or greater duration and before syllables of greater duration have weak stress: /klàb paj-bâan/ 'Went back home'' and p.32 '4) All syllables with short duration have weak stress. Phonemic: /kra'pǎw/ 'pocket' Morphophonemic: /krapǎw/'. The only morphology-linked statements…
morph.elicq: Stress, rhythm and intonation are analysed as prosodic phonemes of utterances (syllable, phrase, clause) from informant speech; no wordlist or instrumental protocol is described. §0.3 p.3: 'CP informants were interviewed entirely in Thai, and ST informants partly in Thai and partly in English.' §1.6.2 p.21 illustrates the six stress contours with utterances: '/!paj/ 'Let's go!' ... /'ɔ̀ɔg paj: khráb/ '(He) went out, sir.'' §4.2.6.3 p.163 contrasts registers: '[/ka-/ and /ca-/] are the only prepositions which have no stressed forms in conversational style, although each is substituted for by stressed forms in citation and in formal style.' §4.5.5 p.219: 'Following are some actual exchanges'.
morph.stmt: Noss: 'The majority of ST morphemes are, in fact, monosyllabic lexemic morphemes' (§2.1.2 p.36); 'Sub-lexemic prefixes are quite rare in ST, and all existing ones are non-productive' (§2.3.1 p.48); 'Sub-lexemic infixes are somewhat more widely distributed in ST than prefixes, and one of them... can actually be said to be productive' (§2.3.2 p.50); in derivation 'it is the first constituent that recurs in many combinations and is productive of new formations. evidence_works.note: Word-level metrical analysis (mono-morphemic polysyllabic words and compounds). States, crediting Luksaneeyanawin (1983, 1993): 'Thai recognizes double stress in a word: primary and secondary. The last syllable always receives primary stress and secondary stress is sometimes suppressed in casual or fast speech' (1998 printing p.63, (25)b). Own tree-building rules (27), p.64-65: 'a. Count syllable weight according to rime-projection. An exception is a word-final CV-syllable which, by its position, is inherently "heavy" despite its internal structure. b. Build right-headed metrical feet with a leftward spreading unbounded foot tree for each foot. c. Build right-headed word-tree with a leftward spreading unbounded word.' Derivation (28) 'dictionary' | - | - | 'where the last syllable receives primary stress' (p.65); (30) 'assigns primary stress to the last syllable [nii] and secondary stress to the first syllable [koo]' (p.66), with casual-speech secondary-stress suppression feeding vowel shortening and reduction. Evidence offered (section 5.2, pp.68-70) is phonological: syllable reduction, syllable and foot deletion. No elicitation procedure or measurement described; examples (7) and (38) taken from Luangthongkum 1977, (26) from Luksaneeyanawin 1993:287; the careful/casual stress patterns of (30)a/b are stated as 'comparable to' Luangthongkum's (1977) careful and casual speech patterns (p.66).

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: Thai has five tones (mid, high, low, falling, rising) and the paper's four perception experiments show listeners identify them from high and low pitch targets aligned to the two moras of a stressed syllable, with falling and rising tones simplified but still identified in connected speech. On stress it restates, citing Bennett 1994, that polysyllabic words and compounds have final stress and that unstressed CV syllables carry only two or three tones, which matches the entry's final-stress rule and tone-and-stress class.

The 6 tone phonemes of ST are defined as follows: Level Tones Plain High /˜/ Constricted High /´/ Mid (unmarked) Low /`/ Oblique Tones Falling /ˆ/ Rising /ˇ/ As far as isolated syllables are concerned, all six tones are in contrast only on syllables with sustained loud stress: /! :/.

Goedemans 1998:248-249 (Appendix D, section VIII header + entry): "VIII Stress is on the first postconsonantal syllable: ... Kuku-thaypan (T192) (ID): Rigsby, Bruce. (1976). Kuku-Thaypan descriptive and historical phonology. In: Peter Sutton (ed.) The languages of Cape York, 68-77. AIATSIS, Canberra." StarLing StressTyp entry for Thaypan: "on first vowel following a consonant".

Onset-conditioned, not positional: stress the first syllable that has an onset (= first postconsonantal syllable / first vowel following a consonant). C-initial words: 10 100 1000...; V-initial words whose second syllable has an onset (the typical shape in this Initial-Dropping language): 01 010 0100...; a word whose first two syllables were both onsetless would take third-syllable stress (unattested in the read data). No single pattern in ^n per length exists, so no reclassification can repair the row.

evidence_works.work: Jenkins 1998, Aspects of Island Tigak Phonology
evidence_works.detail: Describes the ISLAND dialect, explicitly distinct from Beaumont 1979's Central dialect ('Clive Beaumont (1979) wrote a grammar of the central dialect'). Rule: 'The basic stress pattern for Island Tigak words is for stress to fall on the first syllable of a word, unless there is a long vowel or diphthong (forming a complex nucleus) in the second syllable. In the latter case the complex nucleus attracts the stress. Because stress is predictable, it is not indicated orthographically.'. 'This stress rule could be described as "first or heavy stress," whereby the first syllable is stressed unless it is followed by a heavy syllable. Coda consonants are not assigned weight for stress assignment, so only syllables with long vowels or diphthongs are heavy.'. Table 3: 'tug 'to stand', 'ku.tat 'prawn', 'ka.mus 'to finish', 'ti.vu 'grandparent/child', 'ulismung 'whale', 'ta.pu.ogan 'to awake' vs ma.'naas 'hot', sa.'kai 'one', 'viis 'hit', ta.'paak 'leprosy', ku.'ruul 'complete', 'pou.ak 'two'. Prefixation and reduplication leave stress on the root ('stress remains on the first syllable of the root', p. 19: at.'ka.mus, ma.'tug, la.'pou.ak), with a Word Initial Stress Constraint shifting stress to the first syllable when the root stress would land on the third syllable or later ('a.ku.ruul 'completely' in (28), p. 23; 'la.ma.tug 'put/place' in (29)-(30), p. 24), analysed as cyclic stress assignment (29)-(30). Two non-productive prefixes ve- 'related pair' and ta- 'stative' DO take stress ('ve.ti.vu, 'ta.sa.vat, p. 22), 'reanalyzed by the speakers as unaffixed lexemes'; compounds are 'always stressed on the first syllable, even when the second syllable is heavy' ('pa.ngan, 'pa.liu vs pa.'saal, p. 22). Summary p. 23: 'Stress is primarily on the first heavy syllable of a word, with the constraint against (primary) stress occurring more than two syllables from the beginning of the word.' Secondary stress is explicitly left open: 'I have not speculated on the occurrence of secondary stress for the same reason' (lack of data; p. 23), which is consistent with the record's sec_status 'not mentioned in the source'.
evidence_works.loc: Table 3); prefixation (26)); Word Initial Stress Constraint, shift data (28)); Compound Stress Rule (32)-(33)); secondary stress not examined)

356.dq: Words of one, two, or three syllables have stress accent on the first syllable ... Words of more than three syllables generally have primary stress on the first syllable [sec. 2.5] The word is not normally a prosodic entity in Timucua because of the extensive use of external sandhi. ... it is limited to short phrases of compact meaning or to very brief utterances.
356.dloc: Granberry 1956, IJAL 22(2), sec. 2.2 p.102 (sec. 2.5-2.6 p.103 on external sandhi)
356.prule: Granberry 1956 sec. 2.2 (Mocama dialect; all forms from Pareja 1614): stress nonphonemic; words of one to three syllables stressed on the first syllable (yúwu, nípita, árukʷi); longer words generally initial primary plus one secondary on the penult or antepenult; the enclitic conjunctions -tí, -kʷí and dubitive -ku ~ hikú take the primary stress (kùyu-kú 'and fish?', hùlata-ma-kʷí 'and the chief', tìra-hikú 'if it be good'), non-dubitive -ku does not (áku-ku); otherwise the ultima is never stressed. = Pareja 1614 ff.8v-9r: accent on the first vowel in words of one to three vowels, never on the last vowel in longer words, except verbs and some nouns in -hecó/-có, -quí, -maté (elacó, Pedroquí, Pedromaté); non-conjunction -qui and non-interrogative -co leave the accent off the last vowel (tícoco, Píchoco, áyaco). Broadwell 2024 sec.5.6 adopts no fixed rule (Pareja's nahìabotela, mitânicala stressed on the second syllable; attraction suffix-specific; corpus penults before -te, -co, -ta).
356.srule: Not given in Broadwell 2024 sec. 5.6 (pp. 48-53 read), which draws no primary/secondary distinction: the accent-mark differences 'should not be interpreted to show any linguistic difference (such as primary or secondary stress)' (p. 49). Earlier reconstruction, not adopted there: Granberry 1956 sec. 2.2 - in words of four or more syllables one secondary stress on the penult or antepenult (átimùku, tírakùkula), varying between the two (háwìlìču, sec. 2.6); none normally in two- or three-syllable words.
356.quote: At the same time, Pareja also cites forms that do not appear to conform to the generalization about initial stress. ... The data are not completely consistent, but the main pattern is that the affix -hecó ‘if ’ (also written -hêco) attracts stress, as do the affixes -cò and -quì ‘and’, and the sequence of affixes -ma-tê ‘and the’.
356.loc: section 5.6.1 'Pareja's description of stress', pp. 49-50 (section 5.6 'Stress' = pp. 48-53)
356.idn: Timucua (language of the 1612-1635 Franciscan printed texts; no dialect named in Broadwell ch. 5; Granberry 1956 calls Pareja's material the Mocama dialect); data: No fieldwork possible (no speakers since the 18th c.): evidence is accent marking in Pareja's printed works, Mexico 1612-1627…
356.exq_: Use of the enclitic conjunctions -tí (-té), -kʷí (-quí), -ku ~ hikú (-có ~ hecó) and causes the word itself to lose normal stress pattern, primary stress going to the enclitic, e.g. kúyu-ku > kùyu-kú (cuiocó) and fish?, čúwuwù-ti > čùwuwu-tí (chuboboté) and the stars, húlata-mà-kʷi > hùlata-ma-kʷí …

The modern description behind the StressTyp/Gordon coding (Granberry 1956/1993, not open access, not read) is word-based, per Peperkamp 2004:112 fn.21: 'Kager (1995) mentions Timucua as having initial stress, but cliticization interferes with the stress regularity, in that enclitics attract main stress (Granberry 1956).'…
morph.elicq: No speech evidence is possible: Timucua has had no speakers since the 18th century and every stress statement rests on sporadic accent marks in the 1612-1635 Franciscan printed texts. Gatschet 1877:630: 'Pareja does not mark but exceptionally the emphasized syllable of a word, but we can safely assume that the accent rested on the radical syllable...'; Broadwell 2016:3 fn.3: 'In Pareja (1614), the particle is often written with an acute accent, thus <hó>. This may indicate that it attracts stress.' (Coded 'unstated' because none of the enumerated elicitation types applies; the evidence is orthographic/philological, drawn from connected written religious texts.)
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing with a small closed set of verbal prefixes: Gatschet 1877:630 'These latter particles [of relation] are suffixed to the radical syllable and prefixes are seldom found'; Broadwell 2016:6 gives the verb template 'AgrB(applied) applic=AgrB-verb-applic-AgrB-pres-AgrA(general)-past-AgrA(restricted) {complementizer/illoc force}', i.e. only B-set person markers (ni-, chi-), the locative/instrumental applicative na- and the honorific ano-/an- precede the root, while number, benefactive, causative, passive, tense, mood, negation, A-set subject person, question and clause-linking morphology, and all nominal morphology…

XXII, gloss this as 'generally antepenultimate'). 356.cfw: Pareja 1614, Granberry 1956 and Broadwell 2024 agree that the accent falls on the first syllable of words of up to three syllables and never on the last syllable of longer words, with a closed set of enclitics (-hecó, -có, -quí, -maté) drawing it to the end, so the initial default and its morpheme-conditioned exceptions are secure; the only contrary notes are Vinson's 1886 editorial remark that the accent is generally antepenultimate, refuted by the forms printed in his own edition, and the fixed-initial code in StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz and van der Hulst 2015), and everything rests on one 1614 grammar plus a corpus whose accent marks Broadwell 2024 calls sporadic and only partly consistent with it. Mocama dialect of Timucua is described separately below, with a different pattern.

variants.name: Mocama dialect of Timucua (Granberry 1956 after Pareja 1614)
variants.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word at every word length (words of one to three syllables: stress on the first syllable; words of more than three syllables: primary stress on the first syllable); apart from the stress-attracting enclitics the ultima is never stressed (Granberry 1956:102-103).
variants.quote: 2.2. Nonphonemic stress accent characterizes Timucua utterances. Words of one, two, or three syllables have stress accent on the first syllable ... Words of more than three syllables generally have primary stress on the first syllable with secondary stress on the penult or antepenult ... Except in the above cases the ultima never receives stress.

359.prule: Left-anchored, quantity-insensitive, word-domain: initial syllable stressed (rule I; proclitic grammatical monosyllables unstressed, stress on first syllable of lexical host), final syllable never stressed (II), no clash (III), no lapse of three (IV); rightmost stress marginally strongest (VIII). Unique grid at n=2-4: 10, 100, 1010. At n=5-6 code the trisyllabic-feet defaults 10010 and 100100 (dominant-set coding), with a caveat: morphology-conditioned alternates 10100 (2-35f) and 101010 (2-35h, 2-47) are attested and obligatory for their words. n=7 attested as 1010100 in doubly-prefixed forms (2-49, 2-50a) and as 1001010 in a three-member compound (2-52c); no monomorphemic 7-syllable form is given. ViVi (geminate-vowel) sequences count as two syllables for stress purposes; elision-fed final stress/clash are segmental surface exceptions.
359.srule: All stresses before the last one are secondary (rule VIII; grave vs acute in the transcriptions): every word of 4+ syllables has secondary stress on its initial syllable (rule I) with the primary to its right (1010, 10010, 100100 = secondary first, primary last); additional secondaries only where needed to avoid three unstressed syllables in a row without clash (rules III-IV, trisyllabic spacing preferred, e.g. 2-47 101010) and on the initial syllables of stems, disyllabic prefixes/reduplicants and compound members, which keep their own stress (rules V-VI; 2-35h 101010, 2-50a 1010100; a base before a stressed disyllabic suffix keeps 'secondary, rather than primary, stress', p. 22).

360.prule: Primary stress falls on the first vowel of the noun or verb root (SqRR5); inflectional prefixes (š-, la-, wa-, ha-) and clitics/modals are unstressed, so prefixed words are stressed on the root, not the first syllable. In isolation or phrase-finally, PrR2 puts primary stress on a consonant-final last syllable and the root stress reduces to secondary ([.'po.wil.] from #pohwil#, [..po.'wil.] from %pohwil%); Spanish loans keep penultimate stress (PrR1).
360.srule: Derived, not rhythmic: in isolation/phrase-final words the root-initial syllable (primary-stressed phrase-medially) is reduced to SECONDARY stress by Stress Reduction (PrR3) after primary stress is assigned to the final syllable -- [ˌpo.ˈwil] < %pohwil% (three stress levels: primary, secondary, unmarked tertiary). Phrase-medial words carry a single stress; no alternating secondary stresses are described.

morph.stmt: Tojol-ab'al is a head-marking Mayan language with mixed but suffix-leaning affixation: ergative/possessor person (Set A j-/wa-/s-, k-/aw-/y-) and incompletive aspect (x-, la-) are prefixes, while absolutive person, all person-number plurals, status, perfect, mood, voice, noun plural and all derivation (verbalisers, causative -tes, nominalisers, passive/antipassive/anticausative) are suffixes, plus the proclitic determiner ja= and second-position/phrase-final enclitics =xa =to =ni =ma =b'i =i; there is no applicative and no case. 361.prule: Primary stress nearly always falls on the penultimate syllable regardless of the number of syllables in the word (kúma, kumára, bubukólo). Preface p.iv: "This dictionary is the result of two years of living in the Logu Avuavu District of Guadalcanal and of learning and speaking the Tolo language. I am not a linguist and make no pretense of being one. I have however attained a fair degree of fluency in Tolo ... and feel confident that the vocabulary and grammar contained in this book are accurate." 362.tone: Pitch accent per Bright 1964:104 ('a system of pitch accent or tone'; polysyllables show contrastive high-pitch placement, e.g. beešíh 'weevils' vs béebih 'sword fern'; at most two high pitches per word); Bright states no stress placement. Tuttle 1990 (CAIL typescript 'Tolowa Prosody – an Interim Report', pp. 1, 3, 6) says Tolowa 'is not classed as a tone language' and analyses the accent as stress realized by high pitch: domain bounded by the right edge of the stem; stress the last vowel in the domain and all full vowels; rightmost stress strongest; suffixes unstressed — an interim analysis ('predicted … to some extent'). Doty & Guion 2007:107: a preliminary analysis found no pitch accent on unstressed syllables, so 'both stress and pitch accent may be relevant'; in their sample disyllables the stressed syllable is initial in some words and final in others (p. 110). For tone the entry now rests on Bright 1964, quoted in the tone block.

363.quote: §3. Word and sentence prosody. Tonkawa utterances consist of a succession of more or less evenly stressed syllables. In no case does it appear that either stress or pitch accent plays any significant role in the word. Disyllabic forms, however, are generally pronounced with a somewhat heavier stress on the final syllable, whereas in polysyllabic words the main stress moves to the penult. It is my impression that pitch-stress patterns, in kind not unlike those of English, function in Tonkawa phrases and sentences. I do not, however, possess data with which to describe and illustrate this point.

morph.rootq: §1.2 Stress (p.7): 'Stress always falls on the final syllable of the word. Phonetic correlates of stress are greater intensity and higher pitch than preceding syllables: (2) a. [tsi.ˈpup] 'fire.wood' b. [pi.ˈke] 'house' c. [wa.ruʔ.ˈta] 'pumpkin'.' The domain is the word including enclitics, as her transcriptions show stress on case enclitics: {t'ak} + {-ki} > [t'aˈki] 'manioc.bread-Dat' (5a, p.12); /pitaaɬ/ [pitaˈaɬ] 'his/her going.out (Dative)' (1, p.6); and §4.2.2.1 p.141: some auxiliaries have 'one [allomorph] which is stressed and modifies verbs ending in consonants, and another which is cliticized to the verb'.
morph.elicq: No method is stated for the stress description; §1.2 (p.7) supports it only with three isolated citation forms ([tsi.ˈpup] 'fire.wood', [pi.ˈke] 'house', [wa.ruʔ.ˈta] 'pumpkin'), while §1.4.2 (p.14) gives stress-marked whole utterances in 'slow speech: [ni ˈʔits' ˈde ˈha huˈmak ˈma]' vs 'fast speech'. On the data in general (Preface p.xx): 'Some of the examples in the dissertation came from elicitation, and some from texts. For the study, I used oral texts (which were taped and transcribed with the help of consultants) and written texts'. No instrumental measurements are reported.
morph.stmt: 'One of the main characteristics of Trumai is that it is basically an isolating language. There are not many inflectional morphemes and in general words consist of a single morpheme' (ch.2 p.16); 'There is little verbal morphology in Trumai: the verb frequently bears the enclitic -n/-e '3Abs'... Some verbs may bear the prefix wa-... There are no tense-aspect-mood affixes... postverbal particles indicate negation, intensity, and causation' (§3.2 p.98-99). What bound morphology exists is overwhelmingly post-root (NP-final case enclitics, VP-final 3Abs enclitic, cliticized postverbal auxiliaries, nominalizer suffixes, interrogative enclitic); the only prefixes are the kin-term possessor…

tn.quote: 2. Словесное ударение отсутствует. Законы размещения фразового ударения в слове не исследованы. 3. Тон характеризует слоги, или - точнее - мору. Примеры на тоны в односложных словах: H - gač "рог", xa "шерсть"; L - maš "гной", či: "роса"; R - t'ub "палец", vixy "вошь", F - vok "свинья", Xlu "мука". Тоны сильно различаются по употребительности, цифры для односложных слов по нашему словарю таковы: H - 137, L - 33, R - 26, F - 11. Контраст по тону действует лишь на первых двух слогах, на последующих слогах происходит тоновая нейтрализация (ровный тон со ступенчатым понижением к концу).
tn.translation: 2. Word stress is absent. The rules for placing phrasal stress within the word have not been investigated. 3. Tone characterizes syllables, or, more precisely, the mora. Examples of tones in monosyllabic words: H - gač 'horn', xa 'wool'; L - maš 'pus', či: 'dew'; R - t'ub 'finger', vixy 'louse', F - vok 'pig', Xlu 'flour'. The tones differ greatly in frequency; the figures for monosyllabic words in our dictionary are: H 137, L 33, R 26, F 11. The tonal contrast operates only on the first two syllables; on the following syllables tonal neutralization takes place (level tone with stepwise lowering towards the end).
tn.cite: Kibrik, A. E. & S. V. Kodzasov. 1990. Sopostavitel'noe izučenie dagestanskix jazykov. Imja. Fonetika. Moscow: Izdatel'stvo Moskovskogo universiteta. Part III 'Fonetika' by S. V. Kodzasov.
tn.locator: p.344, sketch 18 'Цахурский язык (с. Микик)', 'Слог и просодия' items 2-3; tone labels H/L/R/F defined as two level + two gliding tones on p.318 'Просодия. Акценты'
tn.note: Four tones on the mora: high, low, rising, falling; contrast only in the first two syllables, later syllables neutralized to a level tone stepping down; no word stress (Mikik variety). A second reading (Borise 2018): Mikik variety (Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990) has four tones: high, low, rising, falling; long vowels carry two; contrast only in the first two syllables. Schulze 1997: pitch-marked stress, not tone.

366.cfw: Schulze 1997 and Talibov 2001 describe a dynamic accent that falls on the second syllable of nouns but on the first syllable of verbs, whereas Kodzasov's phonetic study of the Mikik variety (Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990), built on an accented dictionary, finds no word stress at all but a syllable-tone contrast on the first two syllables, so both the type of system and the strict second-syllable placement are contested.

sources.text: Laughlin 1975:23: "Primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables. In the latter instances, the stress is indicated by an acute accent. In normal speech, however, primary stress falls upon the root vowels (on the first, if there are two) and at the end of a phrase." [scan renders the suffix as "-/uA"; rest verbatim.] Corroborating, Aissen 2017:240-1: "At the word level, stress falls on the initial syllable of the root; at the phrase level, it falls on …

Word-level primary stress falls on the root-initial syllable (on the first root vowel if there are two), regardless of preceding prefix syllables — not computable from syllable count. Phrase-level (iP-final) prominence falls on the final syllable of the intonational phrase; a word in isolation is a one-word iP, which is what the surveyed final-at-every-length coding actually captured. Isolation-form final stress additionally has three morphological exception classes (affective verbs in -luh, 1pl-exclusive suffixes, disyllabic reduplicated stems; Laughlin 1975:23).

367.dq: Descriptions of Z Tsotsil characterize prosodic prominence at two levels – the word and the phrase. At the word level, stress falls on the initial syllable of the root; at the phrase level, it falls on the final syllable of the ιP (Laughlin 1975,23; Haviland 1981,14) (stress being predictable, it is not marked in the orthography).
367.dloc: Aissen 2017:241, §3 'Prosodic constraints on =e' (with fn. 7 on the same page), 'Special clitics and the right periphery in Tsotsil', in On looking into words (and beyond), Language Science Press — copy consulted, p.7 (foot-numbered 241); StressTyp2 sister entry; Laughlin 1975:23; Haviland 1981:14
367.prule: Word-level primary stress falls on the root-initial syllable (on the first root vowel if there are two), regardless of preceding prefix syllables — not computable from syllable count. Phrase-level (iP-final) prominence falls on the final syllable of the intonational phrase; a word in isolation is a one-word iP, which is what the surveyed final-at-every-length coding actually captured. Isolation-form final stress additionally has three morphological exception classes (affective verbs in -luh, 1pl-exclusive suffixes, disyllabic reduplicated stems; Laughlin 1975:23).
367.srule: Not mentioned in Laughlin 1975 (Explanatory notes, Phonemics and phonetics, pp. 22-23); Haviland 1981:14 likewise describes only the two levels already in the primary rule (word accent on the first root syllable, stronger phrase-final accent, both carried by a word said alone, e.g. jvábajóm 'musician') and no rhythmic secondary stress.
367.quote: Primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables. In the latter instances, the stress is indicated by an acute accent. In normal speech, however, primary stress falls upon the root vowels (on the first, if there are two) and at the end of a phrase.
367.loc: p. 23 (page; p. 39 of the Smithsonian repository PDF, archive.org leaf n38), Explanatory Notes, sec. 'Phonemics and Phonetics'
367.idn: The passages this record rests on (Laughlin 1975, Haviland 1981, Aissen 2017) describe Zinacantán (San Lorenzo Zinacantán) Tzotzil; StressTyp2's own source for this lect, Weathers 1947, is unread and its variety unverified; Aissen 2017 fn.7 reports the phrase-final prominence for other Tsotsil dialects too…
367.exq_: Primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables. In the latter instances, the stress is indicated by an acute accent.

morph.rootq: Haviland 1981 §1.2 'Stress and Intonation' (English on-line ed.): "The primary accent of a word in Tzotzil falls on the first syllable of the root; there is also an even stronger accent that accompanies the last syllable of a phrase or sentence (it can consists of a single word, pronounced in isolation, or of words uttered in the same breath). ... It is clear that particles are not accented unless they are in final position." (Illustrated with jvabajom 'musician' = j-vAb-aj-om, word accent on the root syllable vab.) Concordant: Laughlin 1975:23: "Primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation except in affective…
morph.elicq: Haviland 1981 §1.2 distinguishes a word 'pronounced in isolation' from 'words uttered in the same breath' and illustrates with recorded examples: "For example, see the following phrases (which can be heard as a .WAV file): jvabajom 'musician' / li jvabajome 'the musician' / Chtal li jvabajome. 'The musician is coming.' ... Here the symbol / represent word, and the symbol // represents phrasal accent". Laughlin 1975:23 likewise contrasts "single words in isolation" with "In normal speech, however, primary stress falls upon the root vowels ... and at the end of a phrase." No instrumental measurements; impressionistic, isolation forms vs connected speech.
morph.stmt: Haviland 1981 §1.1: "The most common form of a Tzotzil root is CVC... Almost all Tzotzil words can be analyzed as a root of this form together with certain affixes.... 367.cfw: Laughlin 1975, Haviland 1981 and Aissen 2017 all describe Zinacantán Tsotsil with two prominences, a stronger one on the last syllable of the phrase, which a word said alone carries and which Laughlin 1975 and Polian 2024 call Tsotsil's final stress, and a weaker one on the first syllable of the root in connected speech, so whether word stress is final or root-initial depends on which prominence one counts as the word's, while the type (fixed, non-contrastive) is not in doubt outside the tonal Carranza dialect described by Polian 2024. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Laughlin 1975 1975.

368.heavy: A syllable containing two or more vowels (a long vowel, i.e. two identical vowels in close transition, or a vowel cluster); primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel (mora) before a juncture, so a word-final (C)VV syllable is stressed (/=tapúu=/, /=igóa=/), otherwise the penult (/=gútu=/, /=tagáta=/).
368.srule: Kuki 1970 posits no separate secondary level, but every juncture-bounded domain of two or three vowels bears its own stress on its penultimate vowel, so words of more than three vowels have more than one stress (/=fára+óa=/ 'flour', /=máa+úi+úi=/ 'painful', /=haére+mái=/ 'come'); the last carries the phrase stress and the others are weaker the further they stand from it. Domain edges (plus juncture) are phonemic: always after a long vowel, never leaving two unstressed vowels adjacent.

morph.stmt: Tuamotuan is a near-isolating Polynesian language in which grammatical categories (TAM, case, article, number, possession, negation, interrogation) are carried by free pre- or post-posed particles ('the full words of a sentence being considered as one does the bricks of a wall, whereas the intervening particles are to them as the mortar', Stimson & Marshall 1964 p.35; 'les mots sont invariables', Annexe 2016 p.33), while the small derivational affix inventory is split: prefixes faka-/haka- (causative), ma- (spontaneity; partialization), to- (partialization), tau- (reciprocity) versus suffixes -hia/-a/-ia/-kia/-tia (passive/'intransitivizing') and -haga/-ga/-raga/-ana/-tana…

morph.elicq: The stress section (§2.3.2 pp.29-32) gives no statement of how stress was observed; its examples range from single words (['ßandɛ] 'rain') to short clauses ([.nɔʔi'ta tɛ kɛ'nɛno] 'He saw his friend.'). The only evidence-type statements are general: "Most materials used in this grammar have been taken from recordings of traditional stories, explanations about how certain aspects of Tukang Besi material and social culture operate, and recordings of conversations." (§1.5 p.12), and for syllabification "native speakers of the language are unanimous in their syllable division ... if asked to break a word up into syllables" (p.29).
morph.stmt: Mixed but verb-heavy morphology with obligatory subject prefixes and valency prefixes before the root and object, applicative, possessive and aspect suffixes after it: "there is much more verbal morphology than there is nominal morphology. 371.dq: Because of sweeping external sandhi phenomena, the smallest phonetic group of Tunica is the phrase, which may contain a single word or several words. Phrases are always set off from other phrases by pauses and are also characterized by special intonational or melodic features. On the other hand, words occurring within the same phrase form a unit. They are not set off from each other by pauses nor…
371.dloc: Haas 1940, Tunica (HAIL 4), ch. I §1.1, p. 13 (archive.org Rosetta Project scan of ch. I pp. 13-15; viewed)
371.prule: No ^n count-only rule exists at any polymorphemic length, so no reclassification is possible. True generalization (Haas 1940, data verified in Bakovic 2016): stress falls on the initial syllable of every stem and of every inherently stressed affix; clash is repaired so stresses are never consecutive (rightward destressing word-internally, stress shift under contraction); when a monosyllabic NOUN stem is preceded by a stressless monosyllabic prefix and followed by a suffix or stem, stress shifts leftward onto the prefix (/?u+'sa+ku/ -> ['?usaku]), while monosyllabic VERB stems retain primosyllabic stress (/?u+'po+wi/ -> [?u'powi]). Surface word patterns: length 3 = 100 or 010; length 4 = 1000, 0100, or 1010 — decided by morphological parse, not syllable count.
371.srule: Source draws no primary/secondary ranking: a word may carry more than one stress -- one on the initial syllable of every stem and of every inherently stressed affix (e.g. ["jaruh"tohku] 'hatchet', ["nara"meli] 'congo snake', ["temi"lEni] 'it is red all about, they say'), never on consecutive syllables (the second of two clashing stresses is removed; leftward shift under contraction). Placement is morphological; no rhythmic (quantity-insensitive) secondary stress is described. Bare stems and stressless-prefix + stem words carry a single stress.
371.quote: Every phrase, every word, and every syllable must begin in a single consonant but may end in a vowel, a consonant, or a cluster of two consonants. Hence vowels are never clustered and clusters of more than three consonants do not occur. A phrase or a word may have one or more stressed syllables but these are never consecutive. ... On the dynamic level, there are two types of syllables, stressed and unstressed. The former are orthographically distinguished from the latter by having an acute sign (') placed after their vowel, e.g., ha'raku "he sings."
371.loc: ch. I Phonology, §1.1 General Remarks, p. 13 (chapter-opening page; following page headed '14 HAAS TUNICA') and §1.22 The Syllabic Phonemes, p. 14

With the addition of affixes of any kind, the stress is on the last syllable, except in the case of words with the question particle –mi, the plural imperative marker –yň/iň and one or two other affixes. e.g: gara'wul ~ garawul'dan; tamamla'mak ~ tamamla'dyňmy; bar'mak ~ 'baryň." morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing/agglutinative: Gray 2004 §1 "It is an agglutinative language i.e. it has a highly developed system of noun and verb suffixes that can produce some very long words indeed" (e.g. Okuwçylaryňkymyka?); Tyson & Clark 1993 p.9 "The meanings of Turkmen words, as well as their grammatical functions within sentences, are indicated by adding elements called suffixes to the ends of the words." No prefixes are described in either source.

qtr.text: 2.1.2. Word stress in Tuvan is dynamic, comparatively weak, and falls, as a rule, on the last syllable of the word: [киъжи́] 'person', [киъжиле́р] 'people', [киъжилерге́] 'to people'. In speech, alongside dynamic stress, musical and quantitative stress may be used (especially to express expressiveness). In the speech flow a function word forms one sound complex with a content word, in which the stress falls on the lexically meaningful word: [чана́͡верген] 'went home', [бажы́ң иъштинде] 'in the house'.

morph.rootq: Harrison 2000 has no dedicated stress section (its acoustic chapter is on distinctive low pitch); its passing statements refer to the word, not the root: p.120 (ch.4 §2.6) 'Nor is it the case that speakers automatically adopt the backness value of vowel of the first (and most prominent) or final (and stressed) syllable'; p.187 (Summary) 'Tuvan employs a number of enclitics. These bound or semi-bound elements lack the morpho-phonological properties of suffixes and are never stressed.' The DB source Sat 1997:386 §2.1.2 likewise states word-final stress with suffixed examples: 'Словесное ударение в Т.я. динамическое, сравнительно слабое, падает, как правило, на последний слог слова: [киъжи]…
morph.elicq: Neither source states the evidence base for the stress claim. Harrison 2000 p.9 (general, not stress-specific): 'The present work is based on field work carried out in Tuva during the period 1996 through 2000 by the author. Data was elicited from many dozens of speakers of various ages, backgrounds, and regions of Tuva'; his instrumental chapter measures pitch/duration, not stress. Sat 1997:386 gives the rule with citation forms and adds only a connected-speech remark: 'В речевом потоке служебное слово со значимым словом образует один звуковой комплекс, в котором ударение падает на лексически значимое слово'…
morph.stmt: Harrison 2000 §2.0 p.18: 'Tuvan, like all Turkic languages, has a primarily agglutinative morphology. The language is almost exclusively suffixing, with each suffix bearing only one piece of grammatical information. Tuvan also has a few morphological processes that are non-agglutinating; these include elision, vowel lengthening, and (partial or full) reduplication.'

tn.quote: Lastly, we raise, but do not definitively resolve, the question of whether Tuvan should be thought of as having a pitch accent or a tone system. We suggest that that low pitch is more akin to tone in its acoustic and phonological behavior. Tuvan would seem to represent, on this view, a paradoxical one-tone language. ... it would have to be construed as a system with just a single ‘tone’, set in a privative opposition to no tone at all. ... Contrastive low pitch is restricted in its distribution to initial syllables and to a subset of the lexicon.
tn.cite: Harrison, K. David. 2000. Topics in the Phonology and Morphology of Tuvan. PhD dissertation, Yale University; Chapter Two 'Distinctive pitch in Tuvan', pp. 53-73 (also read: Sat, Sh. Ch. 1997. Tuvinskij jazyk. Jazyki mira: Tjurkskie jazyki, pp. 385-386)
tn.locator: Chapter Two, section 0 'Introduction', pp. 53-54, and section 2.0 'Contrastive nature of low pitch', p. 56
tn.note: Privative low pitch ('pharyngealized' vowels of earlier work) on initial syllables of a few hundred words, F0-measured; author leans tone over pitch accent, unresolved. Sat 1997: final stress, no tone. A second reading (Dybo et al. 2020): Tuvan 'pharyngealized' vowels analysed as a phonation contrast (modal/slack + creaky, before obstruents) with falling-rising F0; others' pitch analyses cited, not adopted; no tone inventory or stress.

evidence_works.detail: A book review, not a study: it summarises the Novosibirsk monograph and, for the Kaa-Khem subdialect, reports I. D. Dambyra's finding that Russian loans are pharyngealized 'начинающейся с ударного слога и распространяющейся до конца словоформы' (starting from the stressed syllable and spreading to the end of the word-form), with two exceptions: 'однослоги, не имеющие в своей звуковой оболочке консонантных сочетаний' (monosyllables without consonant clusters) and 'неоднослоговые слова с ударением на первом слоге' (polysyllabic words with stress on the first syllable). It does not state a Tuvan word-stress rule; the exception clause implies non-initial stress as the usual case and names initial-stressed polysyllables (a Russian-loan stratum) as the exception class.
